scope: AQA Year 1/AS Pure first school mock only: deduction, exhaustion, counterexample, 2D vectors, graph transformations. No Year 2, Statistics, Mechanics or full historic-paper reproduction.
notes: Five original multi-step applications (38 marks). Mark points are independently authored illustrative marking criteria, not official AQA marking schemes. Automated scores require student review, particularly for alternative methods.

questions.subtopic: Deduction combined with exhaustion of residues
questions.prompt: Prove that n⁵ − n is divisible by 30 for every integer n. You may check the five possible remainders on division by 5, but must also justify divisibility by 2 and 3. [7 marks]
markPoints: The three consecutive integers n−1, n, n+1 include an even integer, so the product is divisible by 2.
One of three consecutive integers is divisible by 3, so the product is divisible by 3.
Write n = 5k+r where r is one of 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, and inspect n⁵−n modulo 5.
For r = 0, 1, 2, the values r⁵−r are 0, 0, 30, all multiples of 5.
For r = 3, 4, the values r⁵−r are 240, 1020, both multiples of 5.
Since n⁵−n has factors 2, 3 and 5, it is divisible by 30 for every integer n.

questions.question: First Maths mock hard challenge
questions.modelAnswer: Factorise n⁵ − n = n(n−1)(n+1)(n²+1). The three consecutive integers n−1, n, n+1 include an even integer, so the product is divisible by 2. One of three consecutive integers is divisible by 3, so the product is divisible by 3. Write n = 5k+r where r is one of 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, and inspect n⁵−n modulo 5. For r = 0, 1, 2, the values r⁵−r are 0, 0, 30, all multiples of 5. For r = 3, 4, the values r⁵−r are 240, 1020, both multiples of 5. Since n⁵−n has factors 2, 3 and 5, it is divisible by 30 for every integer n.

questions.prompt: A student claims: 'For every non-negative integer n, n²+n+17 is prime.' (a) Disprove this with one explicit counterexample. (b) Prove that n²+n+17 is odd for every integer n, and explain why this does not establish that it is always prime. [6 marks]
markPoints: 289 = 17², so this value is not prime.
A single counterexample disproves a claim applying to every non-negative integer.
n²+n = n(n+1), the product of consecutive integers, is even.
Adding 17 makes n²+n+17 odd, but being odd does not guarantee that a number is prime.

questions.question: First Maths mock hard challenge
questions.modelAnswer: Use n = 16 as the counterexample. At n = 16, n²+n+17 = 256+16+17 = 289. 289 = 17², so this value is not prime. A single counterexample disproves a claim applying to every non-negative integer. n²+n = n(n+1), the product of consecutive integers, is even. Adding 17 makes n²+n+17 odd, but being odd does not guarantee that a number is prime.

questions.subtopic: Parameterized collinearity, section ratio and unit direction
questions.prompt: Points A, B, C have position vectors (−2,1), (4,9), (k,k+6). Given that A, B and C are distinct and collinear, find k. Then find AB:BC and the unit vector in the direction AB. Show the vector reasoning rather than relying on a sketch. [8 marks]
markPoints: Collinearity requires AC to be a scalar multiple of AB.
The unit vector along AB is (3/5,4/5), because |AB|=10.
questions.subject: Maths
questions.series: Original first-mock AQA-style Pure Maths challenges
questions.question: First Maths mock hard challenge
questions.modelAnswer: AB = (6,8). AC = (k+2,k+5). Collinearity requires AC to be a scalar multiple of AB. Hence 8(k+2)=6(k+5). Solving gives k=7. BC = (3,4). Since AB=2BC, AB:BC=2:1. The unit vector along AB is (3/5,4/5), because |AB|=10.

questions.subtopic: Midpoint theorem, collinearity and exact magnitude
questions.prompt: Triangle ABC has A=(2,−3), B=(14,5) and C=(−1,8). P is the midpoint of AB; Q is the midpoint of AC. Find P and Q, prove that PQ is parallel to BC using vectors, and find the exact magnitude |PQ|. [8 marks]
markPoints: The midpoint P of AB is (8,1).
The midpoint Q of AC is (1/2,5/2).
PQ = 1/2 BC, which proves PQ is parallel to BC.

questions.question: First Maths mock hard challenge
questions.modelAnswer: AB = (12,8). AC = (−3,11). The midpoint P of AB is (8,1). The midpoint Q of AC is (1/2,5/2). PQ = (−15/2,3/2). BC = (−15,3). PQ = 1/2 BC, which proves PQ is parallel to BC. The magnitude |PQ| is 3√26/2.

questions.subtopic: Reflection, translation, scale factor and exact intercepts
questions.prompt: Let f(x)=x²−6x+5 and g(x)=2f(1−x)−3. (a) Write f in completed-square form. (b) Give a valid sequence of transformations from y=f(x) to y=g(x). (c) Find g in completed-square form, its turning point, its exact x-intercepts and its y-intercept. [9 marks]
markPoints: The turning point of g is (−2,−11).
At x=0, g(0)=−3, so the y-intercept is (0,−3).
questions.subject: Maths
questions.series: Original first-mock AQA-style Pure Maths challenges
questions.question: First Maths mock hard challenge
questions.modelAnswer: f(x) = (x−3)²−4. Reflect y=f(x) in the y-axis. Translate 1 unit right. Stretch vertically by scale factor 2. Translate 3 units down. g(x) = 2(x+2)²−11. The turning point of g is (−2,−11). Setting g(x)=0 gives x = −2 ± √(11/2). At x=0, g(0)=−3, so the y-intercept is (0,−3).
